title: The Low Yield collateral penalty multiplies excess by ten, so a ten-point overshoot erases all allocation profit
content:
A.2.4.1.2.2.1.1.2.3.2 sets the Low Yield Actively Stabilizing Collateral Penalty, "as a percentage of the Total Allocation System Profit," at "the lesser of (1) ten times the Excess Low Yield Actively Stabilizing Collateral Percentage and (2) 100%." A.2.4.1.2.2.1.1.2.3.2.1 defines that excess as the amount by which Low Yield ASC as a share of the Collateral Portfolio exceeds the Minimum Actively Stabilizing Collateral requirement as a share of the same portfolio, and A.2.4.1.2.2.1.1.2.3.2.1.1 defines Low Yield ASC as stabilizing collateral "that earns less than the Agent Credit Line Borrow Rate."

The 10x multiplier is the design. A one-percentage-point overshoot costs 10% of allocation profit; ten points costs everything. The gradient is steep enough that holding excess low-yield collateral is never a marginally bad decision — it is quickly catastrophic to the Prime's earnings.

The behaviour being deterred is subtle. Stabilizing collateral is *required* up to a minimum, so a Prime cannot be penalised for holding it; the penalty targets holding **more** than required in instruments that earn less than the cost of the money funding them. Under the asymmetric profit floor that would otherwise be nearly free — the shortfall lands on Sky — so parking capital in safe, low-yielding assets while keeping upside elsewhere would be a rational play. This penalty prices it.

Capping at 100% of profit rather than allowing a charge beyond it keeps the whole regime one-sided: penalties can zero out a Prime's earnings but never turn settlement into a net loss, preserving the same no-downside property the Distortion Penalty was written to counteract.
description: The penalty is the lesser of ten times the Excess Low Yield Actively Stabilizing Collateral Percentage and 100% of Total Allocation System Profit, making small excesses disproportionately expensive.
